expectedText:
COHABITATION AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

RECITALS — PARTIES AND PURPOSE
This Cohabitation Agreement is made by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee (together, "the Parties"), who state that they are two unmarried adults sharing a household, dated September 1, 2026. The Parties enter into this Agreement to record their mutual understanding regarding the property they own individually and together, the expenses of their shared household, and the financial expectations they hold toward one another during their relationship, separate and apart from any statute or doctrine governing marriage or a registered domestic partnership.

THE MARVIN DOCTRINE — ENFORCEABILITY OF EXPRESS CONTRACTS BETWEEN NONMARITAL PARTNERS
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, under California case law, a court will enforce an express contract between nonmarital partners concerning the property, earnings, and other financial affairs the partners acquire or manage during their relationship, except to the extent the contract is explicitly founded on the consideration of meretricious sexual services. This rule was announced by the California Supreme Court in Marvin v. Marvin (1976) 18 Cal.3d 660, which held that the property-division provisions that apply to married couples do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship, and that such a relationship instead remains subject to distribution under principles the courts themselves develop, including the enforcement of an express contract between the partners.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "We conclude: (1) The provisions of the Family Law Act do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship; such a relationship remains subject solely to judicial decision. (2) The courts should enforce express contracts between nonmarital partners except to the extent that the contract is explicitly founded on the consideration of meretricious sexual services. (3) In the absence of an express contract, the courts should inquire into the conduct of the parties to determine whether that conduct demonstrates an implied contract, agreement of partnership or joint venture, or some other tacit understanding between the parties. The courts may also employ the doctrine of quantum meruit, or equitable remedies such as constructive or resulting trusts, when warranted by the facts of the case."
  — Marvin v. Marvin, 18 Cal.3d 660, 665 (1976) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1148641/marvin-v-marvin/)
  Known gap: This is one state's judicial doctrine — established entirely by the California Supreme Court, not by any statute — used as real evidence of how a court can treat a contract between unmarried cohabitants, not a claim about which state's law, if any, governs a specific couple's cohabitation agreement or that every state enforces this kind of contract the same way. This is one of the most jurisdiction-variable areas of family law: some states enforce express nonmarital cohabitation contracts in essentially the way California does, some require such a contract to satisfy a statutory writing requirement before it is enforceable, some apply significantly more restrictive tests, and some decline to enforce this category of contract at all as a matter of that state's own public policy. This is a single source (the Marvin opinion); no additional independent source was found for this.

IMPLIED CONTRACTS AND EQUITABLE REMEDIES ABSENT AN EXPRESS AGREEMENT
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, under the same California case law, a court is not limited to enforcing an express written or oral contract between nonmarital partners. In the absence of an express agreement, a California court may examine the conduct of the partners to determine whether that conduct demonstrates an implied contract, an implied agreement of partnership or joint venture, or some other tacit understanding between them, and may apply equitable remedies such as a constructive trust or a resulting trust, or allow recovery in quantum meruit for the reasonable value of household services rendered, less the reasonable value of any support received, where a partner rendered those services with the expectation of monetary reward.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "We add that in the absence of an express agreement, the courts may look to a variety of other remedies in order to protect the parties' lawful expectations. The courts may inquire into the conduct of the parties to determine whether that conduct demonstrates an implied contract or implied agreement of partnership or joint venture (see Estate of Thornton (1972) 81 Wn.2d 72 [499 P.2d 864]), or some other tacit understanding between the parties. The courts may, when appropriate, employ principles of constructive trust (see Omer v. Omer (1974) 11 Wash.App. 386 [523 P.2d 957]) or resulting trust (see Hyman v. Hyman (Tex.Civ.App. 1954) 275 S.W.2d 149). Finally, a nonmarital partner may recover in quantum meruit for the reasonable value of household services rendered less the reasonable value of support received if he can show that he rendered services with the expectation of monetary reward. (See Hill v. Estate of Westbrook, supra, 39 Cal.2d 458, 462.)"
  — Marvin v. Marvin, 18 Cal.3d 660, 684-685 (1976) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1148641/marvin-v-marvin/)
  Known gap: This is the same single source as the Marvin doctrine clause above (a different passage of the same 1976 California Supreme Court opinion); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's judicial doctrine, used as real evidence that a court can extend relief to unmarried cohabitants beyond an express contract — not a claim about which state's law, if any, applies to a specific couple, or that every state recognizes these same implied-contract and equitable remedies for unmarried cohabitants. Recognition of implied contracts, constructive or resulting trusts, and quantum meruit claims between unmarried partners varies by state, and some states limit recovery to an express written contract only.

THE MERETRICIOUS-CONSIDERATION LIMIT AND SEVERABILITY
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, under the same California case law, a contract between nonmarital partners is unenforceable only to the extent it is explicitly and inseparably founded on the consideration of sexual services — that is, only where sexual acts form an inseparable part of the consideration for the agreement, so that the agreement is, in substance, a contract for the performance of sexual services. The mere fact that the partners cohabit, or that they have or had a sexual relationship, does not itself invalidate an agreement between them concerning their earnings, property, or expenses, and such an agreement is not invalid merely because the partners contemplated the creation or continuation of their relationship when they entered into it. Where a contract's consideration includes sexual services but is not inseparably based on them, a court may still enforce any severable portion of the contract that is supported by independent, lawful consideration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The fact that a man and woman live together without marriage, and engage in a sexual relationship, does not in itself invalidate agreements between them relating to their earnings, property, or expenses. Neither is such an agreement invalid merely because the parties may have contemplated the creation or continuation of a nonmarital relationship when they entered into it. Agreements between nonmarital partners fail only to the extent that they rest upon a consideration of meretricious sexual services."
  — Marvin v. Marvin, 18 Cal.3d 660, 670-671 (1976) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1148641/marvin-v-marvin/)
  "The decisions in the Hill and Updeck cases thus demonstrate that a contract between nonmarital partners, even if expressly made in contemplation of a common living arrangement, is invalid only if sexual acts form an inseparable part of the consideration for the agreement. In sum, a court will not enforce a contract for the pooling of property and earnings if it is explicitly and inseparably based upon services as a paramour. The Court of Appeal opinion in Hill, however, indicates that even if sexual services are part of the contractual consideration, any severable portion of the contract supported by independent consideration will still be enforced."
  — Marvin v. Marvin, 18 Cal.3d 660, 672 (1976) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1148641/marvin-v-marvin/)
  Known gap: This is the same single source as the two authority clauses above (two further passages of the same 1976 opinion); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's line-drawing test for when a nonmarital-partner contract is unenforceable, used as real evidence of how narrowly one court has drawn that limit — not a claim about which state's test, if any, applies to a specific couple's agreement, or that every state draws the line the same way. Some states apply a broader unenforceability standard to any contract connected to an unmarried couple's sexual relationship, rather than California's narrower explicitly-and-inseparably-founded-on-sexual-services standard.

NO AUTOMATIC SHARING OF PROPERTY BETWEEN UNMARRIED COHABITANTS
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that, under California law, the statutory property-division rules that apply to married spouses do not apply automatically to unmarried cohabitants. The California Supreme Court has held that the provisions of the Family Law Act do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship, and that unmarried partners may, by agreement, choose to pool their earnings and hold property acquired during the relationship in the manner the law governing community property provides, or may instead agree that each partner's earnings and the property acquired from those earnings remains that partner's separate property — meaning that, absent such an agreement, no automatic sharing of property or income between unmarried cohabitants results merely from their living together.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The provisions of the Family Law Act do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship; such a relationship remains subject solely to judicial decision."
  — Marvin v. Marvin, 18 Cal.3d 660, 665 (1976) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1148641/marvin-v-marvin/)
  "In summary, we base our opinion on the principle that adults who voluntarily live together and engage in sexual relations are nonetheless as competent as any other persons to contract respecting their earnings and property rights. Of course, they cannot lawfully contract to pay for the performance of sexual services, for such a contract is, in essence, an agreement for prostitution and unlawful for that reason. But they may agree to pool their earnings and to hold all property acquired during the relationship in accord with the law governing community property; conversely they may agree that each partner's earnings and the property acquired from those earnings remains the separate property of the earning partner. So long as the agreement does not rest upon illicit meretricious consideration, the parties may order their economic affairs as they choose, and no policy precludes the courts from enforcing such agreements."
  — Marvin v. Marvin, 18 Cal.3d 660, 674 (1976) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1148641/marvin-v-marvin/)
  Known gap: This is drawn from the Marvin opinion's own framing (two passages of the same 1976 California Supreme Court opinion already cited above); no additional independent source was found for this despite a search for a later California Court of Appeal restatement. Two candidate later Court of Appeal decisions were checked (Bergen v. Wood (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 854 and Velez v. Smith (2006) 142 Cal.App.4th 1154); both discuss Marvin but only recite its holding rather than independently confirming this default with separate reasoning, so neither was used as a second source here. It is one state's judicial framework, used as real evidence that a default rule of no automatic property-sharing for unmarried cohabitants exists in that state's case law — not a claim about which state's default rule, if any, applies to a specific couple absent an agreement, or that every state has the same default. Some states' common-law-marriage doctrines, domestic-partnership statutes, or other relationship-status statutes may produce a different default outcome for a long-term unmarried couple than California's default of no automatic sharing.

CALIFORNIA HAS NOT CODIFIED THE MARVIN DOCTRINE — STATE VARIATION DISCLOSURE
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that the Marvin doctrine described above has never been enacted into a California statute. The California Supreme Court itself observed that no language in the Family Law Act addresses the property rights of nonmarital partners and that nothing in that act's legislative history suggests the California Legislature considered the subject, and that the rights of nonmarital partners had, before and after the Family Law Act, been fixed entirely by judicial decision rather than by statute. No provision of the California Family Code or Civil Code was located that codifies the Marvin doctrine or otherwise creates a specific statutory cause of action for an unmarried cohabitant's contract or property claim against a partner; the doctrine remains a product of case law that later California appellate decisions can narrow, extend, or depart from without any accompanying change in a statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "No language in the Family Law Act addresses the property rights of nonmarital partners, and nothing in the legislative history of the act suggests that the Legislature considered that subject. The delineation of the rights of nonmarital partners before 1970 had been fixed entirely by judicial decision; we see no reason to believe that the Legislature, by enacting the Family Law Act, intended to change that, state of affairs."
  — Marvin v. Marvin, 18 Cal.3d 660, 681 (1976) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1148641/marvin-v-marvin/)
  Known gap: This is drawn from the Marvin opinion's own framing (a further passage of the same 1976 opinion already cited above), together with an independent check for a codifying statute that did not locate one; a search failure is not proof that no such statute exists, only that this search did not find one, so no additional independent source is claimed here. It is one state's approach — California's choice to leave nonmarital-cohabitant contract and property rights to case law rather than statute — used as real evidence that at least one state takes this approach, not a claim about which state's law, if any, governs a specific couple's cohabitation agreement. Contract and property rights of unmarried cohabitants are widely understood to be one of the most jurisdiction-variable areas of family law in the United States: some states enforce express cohabitation contracts largely as California does; some impose a statutory writing requirement or other formal prerequisites before such a contract is enforceable; some apply a substantially more restrictive test to any contract connected to an unmarried couple's relationship; and some states' courts have declined to enforce this category of contract at all as against that state's public policy. This document does not identify which, if any, of those approaches would apply to a particular couple or in a particular state.

PROPERTY AND EXPENSE SCHEDULE REFERENCE
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee attach and incorporate by reference a Property and Expense Schedule to this Agreement. That Schedule identifies the property each Party owned before the date of this Agreement, which each Party identifies as that Party's separate property, and states the Parties' chosen approach to characterizing property acquired during the relationship as follows: Property acquired jointly will be owned equally; property acquired individually and titled in one partner's name alone remains that partner's separate property. The Schedule also states how the Parties will divide recurring household expenses — including rent or mortgage payments, utilities, groceries, and other shared costs — as follows: Rent and utilities split equally; each partner covers their own individual expenses. An item of property or a category of expense not addressed in the attached Schedule is not governed by this Agreement.

SIGNATURES
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee have executed this Cohabitation Agreement on September 1, 2026.

Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________
